newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stages bridge opening extravaganza.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stages bridge opening extravaganza.

text.p: Hong Kong gave full rein to its party spirit on Sunday by celebrating the opening of a spectacular new suspension bridge in extravagant style, barely a week after a suspected sabotage attempt.

Tens of thousands of people flocked to remote shores to participate in the last big British bash before an exhaustive round of celebrations gets underway to mark the handover of the colony to China in just 65 days.
There was one noticeable absentee from the ranks of Hong Kong society -- future leader Tung Chee-hwa.

Tung, who will step into Governor Chris Patten's shoes when the British depart at midnight on June 30, spent the day in China discussing ways of stemming a tide of illegal child immigrants streaming into the territory.
Fireworks and lasers lit up the night sky in a grand finale to a ceremony which began as a red sun slipped behind the undulating hills of the Kowloon peninsula.

As the shadows lengthened, former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who signed the 1984 treaty governing the handover of Hong Kong to China, declared open what she called "an impressive and inspiring entrance to this modern city".
The bridge links Hong Kong to a new airport taking shape on the island of Lantau and due to open next year.
"Standing here, at Hong Kong's gateway to the world, it (the bridge) is a visible sign of what Hong Kong represents, a rare and fruitful combination of diverse talents and cultures," Thatcher said.

For a moment the graceful span of the world's longest rail-road suspension bridge stood silhouetted against the darkening sky before a filigree of lights snapped on along its 2.14 km (1.33 mile) length.
Curtains of fire dripped down from the bridge-deck -- a pyrotechnic special effect created especially for the HK$5 million ($640,000) display.

Out in the bay bobbed a flotilla of boats. Floating gin palaces, Chinese junks and sanpans, cross-harbour ferries and even dredgers and tugs pressed into service by thousands of sightseers anchored under the watchful eye of the Royal Naval Patrol vessel HMS Starling.
Anxiety about security ran high after cables at the bridge were cut by saboteurs or vandals earlier this month.
Police spokesman Colin Keenan said the authorities had drawn up contingency plans to cover all eventualities -- including guerrilla attacks.

Though pipped for the record of the world's longest suspension bridge -- Britain's Humber bridge holds that honour -- the Tsing Ma bridge is the longest road-rail bridge, satisfying Hong Kong's obsession with superlatives.
Hong Kong people love to boast of having the world's longest outdoor escalator, the world's busiest container port, and of holding the record for the greatest number of Rolls Royce cars per head.
For Hong Kong, the HK$7.2 billion ($920 million) bridge, built by a Japanese-British joint venture and partially assembled in China, marks more than just an engineering feat.

The completion on schedule of a vital -- and very visible -- component in the US$20-billion airport project represents a practical victory over the political row that dogged Sino-British relations on Hong Kong during the countdown.
China denounced the project as extravagant and accused the British of trying to squander Hong Kong's wealth.
The bickering dragged on for more than five years before agreement was finally reached in 1995. But in the meantime, the Hong Kong government quietly got on with the work.
